title: Interactive Dashboards with Plotly
summary: Static charts tell a fixed story, but interactive visualizations let users explore the data themselves, hovering for details, zooming into regions, and filtering to the subset they care about. Plotly is the leading Python library for this: Plotly Exp
content:
# Interactive Dashboards with Plotly

##### The 40 charts nobody needed

An analytics team in Chennai built a sales dashboard with 40 charts. Every metric anyone had ever asked about, on one page, refreshed hourly. It took six weeks.

Usage logs after three months showed the median session lasted 22 seconds. Users opened it, could not find what they wanted, and went back to asking the analyst directly.

The replacement had four charts and two filters. Median session: 4 minutes. Requests to the analyst dropped by roughly 70%.

The failure was not technical. It was a misunderstanding of what a dashboard is for. A dashboard is not a place to put everything you can measure — it is a tool for answering a small number of recurring questions without a human in the loop. Everything else belongs in a report.

Today covers the mechanics of building interactive charts and dashboards, and — more importantly — when interactivity earns its cost.

##### Interactive versus static

| | Static | Interactive |
|---|---|---|
| Author controls | The exact message | The available exploration |
| Reader can | Read | Filter, zoom, hover, drill down |
| Best for | A specific finding, print, slides | Ongoing monitoring, self-service |
| Build cost | Minutes | Hours to days |
| Failure mode | Reader wants a detail you did not show | Reader gets lost with no message |

The decision rule: **static when you are making an argument, interactive when someone needs to answer their own recurring questions.**

Yesterday's storytelling work was entirely static, and correctly so — a presentation has one message and you control it. A dashboard the operations team opens every Monday morning is a different artefact with a different job.

Interactivity genuinely earns its place in four situations: many categories where the user cares about a specific one; dense time series where zooming reveals detail; multi-dimensional data needing a filter; and situations where the data updates and the question stays constant.

##### Plotly Express basics

Plotly Express produces interactive charts in one line, with hover, zoom and pan included by default.

```python
import plotly.express as px
import pandas as pd

df = px.data.gapminder()

fig = px.scatter(
    df.query("year == 2007"),
    x="gdpPercap", y="lifeExp",
    size="pop", color="continent",
    hover_name="country",
    hover_data={"pop": ":,.0f", "gdpPercap": ":$,.0f", "year": False},
    log_x=True, size_max=55,
    labels={"gdpPercap": "GDP per capita (USD, log scale)",
            "lifeExp": "Life expectancy (years)"},
    title="Wealth and life expectancy, 2007",
)
fig.update_layout(template="plotly_white", height=550)
fig.show()
```

Four variables in one chart — x, y, size, colour — plus a fifth in the hover tooltip. `hover_data` with format strings controls exactly what appears and how it is formatted, which is where much of the value lives: **the tooltip is where you put detail that would clutter the chart.**

The core chart types mirror Matplotlib:

```python
px.line(df, x="date", y="revenue", color="region", markers=True)
px.bar(df, x="city", y="orders", color="segment", barmode="group")
px.histogram(df, x="amount", nbins=40, color="channel", marginal="box")
px.box(df, x="region", y="delivery_min", points="outliers")
px.imshow(corr_matrix, text_auto=".2f", color_continuous_scale="RdBu_r",
          zmin=-1, zmax=1)
px.treemap(df, path=["region", "city", "store"], values="revenue")
px.choropleth(df, locations="iso_alpha", color="value", hover_name="country")
```

Two Plotly Express features with no simple Matplotlib equivalent:

```python
# Faceting — small multiples in one call
px.scatter(df, x="gdpPercap", y="lifeExp", facet_col="continent",
           facet_col_wrap=3, log_x=True, height=650)

# Animation over time
px.scatter(df, x="gdpPercap", y="lifeExp", animation_frame="year",
           animation_group="country", size="pop", color="continent",
           log_x=True, range_x=[100, 100_000], range_y=[25, 90], size_max=55)
```

Setting `range_x` and `range_y` explicitly on an animation matters — without fixed axes the scale jumps every frame and the movement becomes impossible to read.

For finer control, `plotly.graph_objects` gives you the full API:

```python
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

fig = make_subplots(rows=2, cols=1, shared_xaxes=True,
                    row_heights=[0.7, 0.3], vertical_spacing=0.08,
                    subplot_titles=("Revenue", "Order count"))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=d.date, y=d.revenue, name="Revenue",
                         line=dict(width=2)), row=1, col=1)
fig.add_trace(go.Bar(x=d.date, y=d.orders, name="Orders",
                     marker_color="#a0aec0"), row=2, col=1)
fig.update_layout(height=650, template="plotly_white", hovermode="x unified")
```

`hovermode="x unified"` shows all series' values at one x position in a single tooltip — genuinely useful for time series comparison and worth knowing.

##### Interactivity that helps

Plotly gives you hover, zoom, pan and legend-click filtering for free. Some additions worth making deliberately:

```python
# Range selector buttons and a range slider for time series
fig.update_xaxes(
    rangeslider_visible=True,
    rangeselector=dict(buttons=[
        dict(count=7, label="7d", step="day", stepmode="backward"),
        dict(count=1, label="1m", step="month", stepmode="backward"),
        dict(count=3, label="3m", step="month", stepmode="backward"),
        dict(step="all", label="All"),
    ]),
)

# Annotate the point that matters — interactivity does not replace a message
fig.add_annotation(x="2026-10-20", y=9.2, text="Diwali campaign",
                   showarrow=True, arrowhead=2, ax=-60, ay=-40)
fig.add_hline(y=5.0, line_dash="dash", line_color="grey",
              annotation_text="Target")
```

That annotation is the important habit. Interactivity lets users explore, but they still need to know what you want them to notice first. **An interactive chart without a default message is a maze.**

Two things to avoid: `updatemenus` dropdowns that toggle traces (users rarely find them, and they hide data), and animations for anything other than genuine time evolution.

##### Building a dashboard with Streamlit

Streamlit turns a Python script into a web app with no HTML or JavaScript. It is the fastest path from analysis to shareable tool.

```python
# app.py
import streamlit as st
import pandas as pd
import plotly.express as px

st.set_page_config(page_title="Sales Dashboard", layout="wide",
                   initial_sidebar_state="expanded")

@st.cache_data(ttl=3600)                      # cache: do not reload on every interaction
def load_data():
    df = pd.read_parquet("data/sales.parquet")
    df["date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["date"])
    return df

df = load_data()

# ---- Sidebar filters ----
st.sidebar.header("Filters")
regions = st.sidebar.multiselect("Region", sorted(df.region.unique()),
                                 default=sorted(df.region.unique()))
date_range = st.sidebar.date_input("Date range",
                                   value=(df.date.min(), df.date.max()),
                                   min_value=df.date.min(), max_value=df.date.max())
min_amount = st.sidebar.slider("Minimum order value (₹)", 0, 50_000, 0, step=500)

mask = (df.region.isin(regions)
        & df.date.between(pd.Timestamp(date_range[0]), pd.Timestamp(date_range[1]))
        & (df.amount_inr >= min_amount))
d = df[mask]

if d.empty:
    st.warning("No data matches these filters. Try widening the range.")
    st.stop()

# ---- KPI row ----
st.title("Sales Performance")
c1, c2, c3, c4 = st.columns(4)
prev = df[mask & (df.date < pd.Timestamp(date_range[0]) + pd.Timedelta(days=30))]
c1.metric("Revenue", f"₹{d.amount_inr.sum()/1e7:.2f} Cr",
          delta=f"{(d.amount_inr.sum()/max(prev.amount_inr.sum(),1) - 1):.1%}")
c2.metric("Orders", f"{len(d):,}")
c3.metric("Avg order value", f"₹{d.amount_inr.mean():,.0f}")
c4.metric("Unique customers", f"{d.customer_id.nunique():,}")

# ---- Linked charts ----
left, right = st.columns([3, 2])
with left:
    daily = d.groupby(d.date.dt.date, as_index=False).amount_inr.sum()
    st.plotly_chart(
        px.line(daily, x="date", y="amount_inr", title="Daily revenue",
                labels={"amount_inr": "Revenue (₹)"}).update_layout(
            template="plotly_white", height=380),
        use_container_width=True)

with right:
    by_region = d.groupby("region", as_index=False).amount_inr.sum() \
                 .sort_values("amount_inr")
    st.plotly_chart(
        px.bar(by_region, x="amount_inr", y="region", orientation="h",
               title="Revenue by region").update_layout(
            template="plotly_white", height=380),
        use_container_width=True)

with st.expander("View underlying data"):
    st.dataframe(d.head(500), use_container_width=True)
    st.download_button("Download filtered CSV", d.to_csv(index=False),
                       "filtered_sales.csv", "text/csv")
```

```bash
streamlit run app.py
```

The mechanics: Streamlit re-runs the entire script top-to-bottom on every interaction. That model is simple and it means **`@st.cache_data` is essential** — without it, a 2 GB parquet file reloads every time someone moves a slider, and the app becomes unusable.

Three details that separate a usable dashboard from a frustrating one. The **empty-state check** with `st.stop()` — filter combinations that return nothing are common, and an unhandled empty DataFrame produces a stack trace. The **download button**, because someone always wants the data in Excel. And **`use_container_width=True`**, so charts resize properly.

**Plotly Dash** is the alternative when you need more control — explicit callbacks, multi-page routing, and production authentication. The trade-off is verbosity: Dash requires you to wire every interaction explicitly, where Streamlit infers it. For a data scientist building an internal tool, Streamlit is almost always the right choice; Dash makes sense for a polished product with complex interaction logic.

##### Dashboard design principles

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Should this be a dashboard?] --> B{Recurring question?}
    B -->|No, one-time finding| C[Static report or slides]
    B -->|Yes| D{Who uses it and how often?}
    D -->|Daily monitoring| E[3-5 KPIs + 2-4 charts, one screen]
    D -->|Occasional exploration| F[Filters + linked charts + data export]
    E --> G[Design rules]
    F --> G
    G --> H[Most important metric top-left]
    G --> I[Every chart answers a stated question]
    G --> J[Filters in a sidebar, defaults sensible]
    G --> K[Loads in under 3 seconds]
```

The rules that would have saved the Chennai team:

**Start from the questions, not the data.** Write down the five questions the dashboard must answer. If a chart does not answer one of them, it does not belong. Forty charts means nobody wrote the questions down.

**Fit on one screen.** Scrolling means the layout failed. If you genuinely need more, use tabs or pages.

**Top-left is the most valuable real estate.** Western reading order puts attention there — put the headline metric there.

**Default to the common case.** Most users want "this month, all regions". Make that the default state so the dashboard is useful before anyone touches a filter.

**Show context, not bare numbers.** "₹2.3 Cr" means nothing alone. "₹2.3 Cr, +12% vs last month, 94% of target" means something. Streamlit's `st.metric` with a `delta` does this for free.

**Performance is a feature.** Cache aggressively, pre-aggregate before loading, and query only the rows you need. A dashboard taking eight seconds to respond to a filter will be abandoned.

**Label everything.** Units, time ranges, and a "data as of" timestamp. Dashboards get screenshotted and forwarded with no context.

```python
st.caption(f"Data as of {df.date.max():%d %b %Y} · Updated hourly · "
           f"Source: sales_warehouse.orders")
```

##### Deploying

```bash
pip freeze > requirements.txt
git init && git add . && git commit -m "sales dashboard"
# Push to GitHub, then connect the repo at share.streamlit.io
```

Streamlit Community Cloud deploys free from a public GitHub repository. Secrets go in the app settings, never in the code:

```python
db_url = st.secrets["DATABASE_URL"]
```

For anything containing real business data, use authentication and a private deployment. A public Streamlit URL is genuinely public, and dashboards accidentally exposing customer data is a recurring incident.

##### Common mistakes

- Building a dashboard when a one-off report was the right answer.
- Forty charts and no stated questions.
- No caching, so every interaction reloads the full dataset.
- Filter combinations producing an empty DataFrame and a stack trace.
- Interactivity substituting for a message — no annotations, no defaults, no guidance.
- Metrics with no comparison, target or context.
- No "data as of" timestamp on a dashboard that gets screenshotted.
- Charts that require scrolling to compare.
- Animation used for something that is not time evolution.
- Deploying business data to a public URL.

##### Hands-on

Recreate three static charts from an earlier day as interactive Plotly Express figures, adding meaningful hover data with proper formatting and at least one annotation marking the key finding. Then build a small Streamlit app combining them with a sidebar filter, a KPI row using `st.metric` with deltas, caching on the data load, and an empty-state guard. Run it locally and interact with it as a user would — the friction you notice in the first thirty seconds is what your users will notice too.

For the mini-project, build an interactive dashboard where filtering by a category updates multiple linked charts. Before writing any code, write down the five questions it must answer and design backwards from those. Include KPIs with context, at least three charts, a data-export button, a "data as of" caption, and sensible defaults so it is useful on first load. Deploy it to Streamlit Community Cloud and get a shareable link. Then have someone else use it without explanation and note where they hesitate.

For the assignment, take a static report and identify which two charts genuinely benefit from interactivity and which are better left static. Justify each with reference to the decision rule — is the reader making an argument or answering their own recurring question? The charts that should stay static are usually the ones carrying your main finding.

##### Key takeaways

- Static charts make an argument; interactive dashboards answer recurring questions. Choose by which job you have.
- Plotly Express gives four-plus dimensions and free hover, zoom and legend filtering in one line.
- `@st.cache_data` is mandatory in Streamlit — the script re-runs entirely on every interaction.
- Design from the five questions the dashboard must answer, fit it on one screen, and default to the common case.
- Interactivity does not replace a message — annotate the finding and give context to every metric.
